analogy.p: **Filtration** is like a net with holes that lets small fish through but keeps big ones. **Chromatography** is like a race on a sticky track: runners (substances) that are easily carried (soluble) and don't stick to the track move furthest, others lag behind. **Distillation** is like sending children out on a hill one at a time: lighter ones (lower boiling point) run off first. The comparison breaks down because particles do not choose to move; their behaviour depends on forces between particles and on energy.

bullets: The five methods in the spec are **filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation, fractional distillation and chromatography**.
Filtration uses a difference in **particle size / solubility** (insoluble solid versus liquid).
Crystallisation and simple distillation use the difference between a **dissolved solid** and the **solvent** (non-volatile versus volatile).
Fractional distillation uses different **boiling points** of liquids that mix.
Chromatography uses different **solubility in the solvent** and different attraction to the paper.
A compound cannot be separated by these methods; it needs a chemical reaction.
The first step in any question is to **identify the type of mixture** and the property that differs.
core.h: 1. Why mixtures can be separated physically
core.p: In a mixture the substances are **not chemically combined**, so each keeps its own **physical properties**, such as particle size, solubility and boiling point. Separation techniques make use of a **difference in one of these properties**. Because no chemical bonds are broken or made, **no new substances are formed** and the substances you collect are the same as those you started with. This is what makes these **physical processes** rather than chemical reactions.

bullets: **Insoluble solid + liquid** (e.g. sand in water): filtration.
**Soluble solid + solvent, want the solid** (e.g. salt from salt solution): crystallisation (or evaporation).
**Soluble solid + solvent, want the solvent** (e.g. pure water from seawater): simple distillation.
**Mixture of liquids that mix** (e.g. ethanol and water): fractional distillation.
**Mixture of coloured substances** (e.g. inks, food dyes): paper chromatography.
**Soluble + insoluble solids** (e.g. rock salt, sand and salt): dissolve in water, filter, then crystallise the filtrate.
Always say **why**: 'because the sand is insoluble and its particles are too big to pass through the filter paper'.
core.p: Exam questions give you a mixture and ask which technique to use. The decision rests on whether each substance is a **solid, liquid or dissolved**, and whether it is **soluble or insoluble**. Work through the logic systematically, then justify your choice with the property that is different.

bullets: Method: fold filter paper into a cone, place in a funnel over a conical flask, pour the mixture in slowly.
Residue is the **insoluble solid** left on the filter paper; it can be washed with distilled water to remove traces of filtrate and then dried.
Filtrate may still contain **dissolved** substances; these are not removed by filtering.
Filtration does **not** separate a dissolved solid from its solvent because the dissolved particles are as small as the solvent particles and pass straight through.
Example: sand and water; chalk (calcium carbonate) from a reaction mixture; copper oxide from copper sulfate solution in salt preparations.
Vacuum filtration (Buchner funnel) speeds the process up by sucking liquid through.
Link: filtration is used in water treatment to remove solids and in preparing soluble salts, where excess insoluble reactant is filtered off.
core.p: **Filtration** separates an **insoluble solid** from a liquid or solution. The mixture is poured through **filter paper** held in a funnel. The tiny holes in the paper allow the liquid (and any dissolved substances) to pass through but are **too small for the solid particles**. The solid collected on the paper is the **residue** and the liquid that passes through is the **filtrate**.

bullets: Step 1: gently heat the solution in an **evaporating basin** to evaporate **some** of the solvent. Do not boil off all the water.
Step 2: test whether the solution is ready by dipping a **glass rod** in and removing it; if small crystals form on the rod as it cools, the solution is saturated (the point of crystallisation).
Step 3: leave the solution to **cool slowly** at room temperature; slow cooling forms **larger crystals**.
Step 4: **filter** off the crystals, wash with a **small amount of cold distilled water**, then dry them between sheets of filter paper or in a warm oven.
Why not evaporate to dryness? Some solids **decompose** or lose water of crystallisation when overheated, and the solid can spit or be left impure.
Cold water is used for washing so that **little of the product re-dissolves**.
Link: crystallisation is the last step when making soluble salts such as copper sulfate crystals.
core.p: **Crystallisation** is used to obtain a **soluble solid** from its solution. The solvent is partly evaporated to make a **saturated solution**, which is then cooled so the solid comes out of solution as **crystals** because the solubility of most solids falls as temperature falls. This method is preferred to evaporating to dryness because it gives larger, purer crystals and avoids damaging the solid.

bullets: Apparatus: round-bottomed flask, heat source, **thermometer** at the side arm, **Liebig condenser**, collection beaker.
The **thermometer bulb** is placed at the level of the side arm to measure the temperature of the vapour; it should read the **boiling point of the solvent** (100 °C for water).
Cooling water goes in at the **bottom** and out at the **top** of the condenser so that the jacket fills completely and cooling is efficient.
Anti-bumping granules or boiling chips can be added to give smooth boiling.
The dissolved **solute remains** in the flask as it is not volatile.
Do not distil to dryness; stop when little liquid remains.
Used to produce **drinking water** from seawater, though it needs a large amount of energy so it is costly.
core.p: **Simple distillation** separates a **solvent from a solution**, for example pure water from salt solution. The solution is heated until the solvent **evaporates**, the vapour travels into a **condenser** where it is cooled and **condenses** back to a liquid, and the pure liquid (the **distillate**) is collected. The dissolved solid has a much higher boiling point so it stays behind in the flask.

bullets: Ethanol has the lower boiling point (78 °C) so it **evaporates first** and reaches the top of the column; water remains mostly in the flask.
The **glass beads give a large surface area** for repeated evaporation and condensation, improving separation.
The thermometer at the top of the column reads about **78 °C** while ethanol is distilling.
When the ethanol has gone, the temperature rises towards 100 °C; the collection vessel is changed to collect the **water**.
Each substance collected is called a **fraction**.

Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons separated by fractional distillation in a fractionating column that is hot at the bottom and cool at the top, so hydrocarbons with larger molecules and higher boiling points are drawn off lower down.
Compared with simple distillation, fractional distillation is **better at separating liquids whose boiling points are close together**.
core.p: **Fractional distillation** separates a mixture of **miscible liquids** that have **different boiling points**, such as ethanol (78 °C) and water (100 °C). The mixture is heated and the vapours rise up a **fractionating column** filled with glass beads. The column is **hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top**, so the vapour of the liquid with the higher boiling point **condenses and runs back down**, while the vapour of the liquid with the lower boiling point continues to the top and into the condenser.

bullets: Simple: no column; fractional: **fractionating column** between flask and condenser.
Simple separates **solute from solvent** (or liquids with very different boiling points); fractional separates **liquids with different boiling points**.
Both rely on **evaporation then condensation**.
The substance with the **lowest boiling point** is collected first in both.
Both need heat energy, so they have **high energy costs** on an industrial scale.
core.p: These two are often confused. **Simple distillation** has a single evaporation and condensation and is suited to a **big difference in boiling point**, such as a dissolved solid and its solvent. **Fractional distillation** includes a column that causes many cycles of evaporation and condensation, so it can separate **mixtures of liquids with similar boiling points**.

bullets: Draw the baseline in **pencil** (pencil does not dissolve in the solvent; ink would run and spoil the result).
The baseline must be **above the solvent level** or the spots would wash into the solvent.
Put on small spots of each sample and label them; let each dry.
Place the paper in a beaker with a little solvent and put a lid on it to stop the solvent evaporating.
Remove the paper **when the solvent front is near the top** and mark the solvent front immediately in pencil, then leave to dry.
Use **water** for water-soluble substances (food colourings); some inks need **ethanol or another organic solvent**.
The result, a **chromatogram**, shows one spot for a **pure** substance and **more than one spot** for a mixture.
core.p: **Chromatography** separates **small amounts of coloured substances**, such as inks, dyes and food colourings. A spot of the mixture is placed on a **baseline** on chromatography paper, and the paper stands in a **solvent**. The solvent soaks up the paper (the **mobile phase**), carrying substances with it. Substances that are **more soluble in the solvent** and **less attracted to the paper** (the stationary phase) travel **further up** the paper.

bullets: **Rf has no units** because it is a ratio of two distances.
Rf is always **between 0 and 1** because a substance cannot move further than the solvent.
The same substance in the same solvent always gives the **same Rf value**, so Rf values can be matched to data tables to identify substances.
A **pure** substance gives **one spot**; a mixture gives **two or more** spots.
If a sample spot is level with a known reference spot, the sample could contain that substance.
A spot that stays on the baseline is not soluble in that solvent or very strongly attracted to the paper.
Rearrangement: distance moved by substance = Rf × distance moved by solvent.
core.p: A chromatogram shows how many substances a sample contains and can be used to identify them by comparing to **known reference substances** run at the same time. The **Rf value** (retention factor) is a number that compares how far a substance travelled with how far the solvent travelled. **Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent.** Both distances are measured from the **baseline**, and the substance distance is measured to the **centre of the spot**.

bullets: The **mobile phase** is the solvent; the **stationary phase** is the paper.
Higher solubility in solvent means higher Rf value.
Using a different solvent changes the Rf values, so Rf must be compared only in the **same solvent**.
Pencil is used because a pen ink would itself separate and confuse the result.
Chromatography can show if a food has banned colours or if an ink is a mixture of dyes, which is useful in forensic and food analysis.
Chromatography needs only a tiny amount of sample.
core.p: Each substance in the mixture is partly **dissolved in the moving solvent** and partly **attracted to the stationary paper**. A substance that dissolves well in the solvent and sticks weakly to the paper is carried far; one that dissolves poorly and sticks strongly moves a short distance. Because every substance has its own balance, the substances end up at **different heights** and so become separated.

bullets: Step 1: crush rock salt and add to **warm water** in a beaker; stir to dissolve the salt (sand does not dissolve).
Step 2: **filter**; sand is the residue, salt solution is the filtrate. Wash and dry the sand.
Step 3: pour the filtrate into an **evaporating basin** and **heat gently** to evaporate some water.
Step 4: when crystals form on a glass rod, **stop heating** and leave to cool and crystallise.
Step 5: filter the crystals, wash with a little cold water, **dry**.
If you want pure water as well, **simple distillation** of the filtrate would give it.
For a three-component mixture such as iron, sand and salt, use a **magnet** first, then dissolve and filter the rest.
core.h: 11. Separating a mixture of several substances
core.p: Real problems often involve more than one technique used in a **sequence**. A standard example is **rock salt**, which is salt mixed with insoluble sand. Because only the salt is soluble, you can use water to separate them: **dissolve, filter, then crystallise**. Keep a logical order and state what is collected at each stage.

bullets: Wear **eye protection** and tie back long hair.
Ethanol is **flammable** so use an electric heater or water bath rather than a Bunsen burner.
The apparatus must be **open at the receiving end** so that pressure does not build up.
Use a **heat-proof mat** and allow glassware to cool before handling.
Link to **water treatment**: filtration then chlorination for potable water, and distillation to desalinate seawater.
Link to **crude oil**: fractional distillation on a large scale.
Link to **electrolysis and analysis**: purity tests rely on knowing pure substances have fixed melting/boiling points.
core.p: After separating, you may be asked to check purity. A **pure substance** melts and boils at a **fixed temperature**, so measuring the melting or boiling point is a test: a **sharp** melting point shows purity while a **range** shows a mixture. Safety matters in distillation: never heat a closed system, take care with hot glassware, and keep **flammable** liquids such as ethanol away from naked flames (use a hot water bath or electric heater).

exam: **'State' questions (1 mark):** name the technique, e.g. 'filtration', 'fractional distillation'.
**'Suggest a method' (2 marks):** name the method plus the property reason, e.g. 'filtration because sand is insoluble'.
**Method questions (4-6 marks):** give **ordered steps**, include apparatus (evaporating basin, filter paper, glass rod), say what is collected at each stage, and mention **drying**.
**Crystallisation**: say 'heat to evaporate **some** water', 'leave to cool', 'crystals form', 'filter', 'dry'.
**Distillation diagrams:** label flask, thermometer, condenser, **water in at bottom and out at top**, distillate.

**'Explain how fractional distillation works' (4 marks):** heated, vapours rise, column hotter at bottom cooler at top, higher boiling point liquid **condenses and returns**, lower boiling point liquid reaches the top and is collected.
**Chromatography reasons:** pencil, baseline above solvent, lid to stop evaporation, solvent front marked.
**Rf calculations (2-3 marks):** write the formula, substitute, answer to 2 significant figures **without units**.
**Identifying substances:** compare spots **level with known samples**, and state that the same substance has the same Rf in the same solvent.
**Pure or mixture from chromatography:** one spot = pure; more than one = mixture. Say 'at least' because two substances could travel the same distance.
**Marks come from specific terms:** residue, filtrate, saturated, condenser, boiling point, soluble.

mistakes.r: Dissolved particles are tiny and pass through the filter paper; use **crystallisation or distillation**.
mistakes.w: Saying filtration separates salt from salt solution.

mistakes.r: Heat only until saturated (crystals on glass rod), then **cool slowly** to form crystals.
mistakes.w: Evaporating the solution to dryness to get crystals.

mistakes.r: Use **pencil**, because pencil is insoluble in the solvent.
mistakes.w: Using a ballpoint pen for the baseline in chromatography.

mistakes.r: The baseline must be **above the solvent** so that the spots do not dissolve into the solvent.
mistakes.w: Putting the baseline below the solvent level.

mistakes.r: Rf has **no units** since it is a ratio.
mistakes.w: Giving Rf units such as cm.

mistakes.r: Measure from the **baseline** to the **centre of the spot**, and baseline to the **solvent front**.
mistakes.w: Measuring the Rf distance from the bottom of the paper.

mistakes.r: Water enters at the **bottom** and leaves at the **top** so the jacket stays full.
mistakes.w: Water in at the top of the condenser.

mistakes.r: The vapour is **condensed** and collected; this is evaporation then condensation.
mistakes.w: Saying distillation 'removes' water by boiling it away and gives no vapour.

mistakes.r: It works because of different **boiling points**; no chemical reaction takes place.
mistakes.w: Saying fractional distillation works because the liquids 'react' or 'burn' at different temperatures.

summary: AQA wants you to know that mixtures can be separated by physical processes (filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation, fractional distillation and chromatography) that involve no chemical reaction and make no new substances. You must be able to choose the right method for a given mixture, describe the apparatus and method, and explain why it works, including calculating Rf values in chromatography.

terms.d: A physical process that separates an insoluble solid from a liquid using filter paper.
The solid left on the filter paper after filtration.
The liquid that passes through the filter paper.
A process that obtains a soluble solid from its solution by evaporating some solvent and cooling to form crystals.
A solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature.
A process that separates a solvent from a solution by evaporation followed by condensation.
A process that separates a mixture of liquids with different boiling points using a fractionating column.
The liquid collected after condensation in distillation.
Apparatus that cools vapour so that it turns back into a liquid.
A column, often filled with glass beads, hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top, that separates liquids by boiling point.
A method of separating mixtures by their different solubilities in a solvent and attraction to a stationary phase.
The solvent that moves through the paper in chromatography.
The paper (or other material) that does not move in chromatography.
Distance moved by substance divided by distance moved by solvent; it has no units.
The furthest point reached by the solvent on the chromatography paper.
Liquids that mix completely to form one layer.
Able / unable to dissolve in a particular solvent.

worked.ans: Add the rock salt to water and stir to dissolve the salt. Filter the mixture; the insoluble sand stays on the filter paper as the residue and the salt solution passes through as the filtrate. Wash the sand with distilled water and dry it. Gently heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin to evaporate some of the water until a saturated solution forms (crystals appear on a glass rod). Allow to cool slowly so that crystals form, filter off the crystals and dry them between filter paper.
worked.q: A student has a mixture of sand and salt (rock salt). Describe how she could obtain pure dry salt crystals and a sample of sand. (6 marks)
steps: Dissolve: add the mixture to water and stir so salt dissolves; sand does not.
Filter: pour through filter paper; sand is the residue, salt solution the filtrate.
Crystallise: heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin to evaporate some water until crystals form on a glass rod.
Leave to cool, filter off the crystals, dry them between filter paper.

worked.ans: Rf of A = 0.40; Rf of B = 0.60 (no units). The unknown sample gives spots at the same Rf values as A and B, so it is a mixture containing both A and B.
worked.q: In a chromatography experiment the solvent front moved 12.0 cm. Substance A moved 4.8 cm and substance B moved 7.2 cm from the baseline. Calculate the Rf values and say whether an unknown sample with spots at 4.8 cm and 7.2 cm contains both. (4 marks)
steps: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent.
The unknown has spots at the same distances with the same solvent, so the same Rf values 0.40 and 0.60.

worked.ans: Use fractional distillation. Heat the mixture so the liquids evaporate and the vapours rise up the fractionating column, which is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top. Water, with the higher boiling point, condenses and runs back into the flask. Ethanol, with the lower boiling point of 78 °C, reaches the top, passes into the condenser, condenses and is collected as the distillate.
worked.q: Ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) and water (100 °C) are mixed. Explain how to separate them. (4 marks)
steps: Identify: miscible liquids with different boiling points, so fractional distillation.
Heat: vapours rise into the fractionating column.
Column: hotter at bottom, cooler at top; water vapour condenses and runs back.
Ethanol (lower boiling point) reaches the top at 78 °C, goes into the condenser and is collected.
